questions.stem: The Bank of Canada raises its policy interest rate to reduce inflation. According to the lesson, which short-run consequence is most likely?
questions.successCriteria: Student recognizes that lowering inflation through higher interest rates can temporarily raise unemployment.
questions.ossdExpectation: Analyse various aspects of monetary policy in Canada and their impact on the economy.
questions.alignmentNote: Monetary policy goals and their trade-offs are central to analysing the Bank of Canada's monetary policy.
questions.stemIntent: Checks whether students understand that monetary policy goals conflict in the short run, specifically the unemployment cost of disinflation.
questions.commonMisconception: All six monetary policy goals can be achieved simultaneously without any trade-offs, or inflation control has no employment cost.

options.label: A
options.text: Unemployment immediately falls because lower inflation boosts consumer spending.
options.feedbackWrong: Disinflation usually does not immediately boost employment; the lesson explicitly notes that raising rates to curb inflation may temporarily increase unemployment.

options.label: B
options.text: Unemployment may temporarily rise, reflecting a trade-off between lower inflation and employment.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The lesson states that policy targets can conflict in the short run; disinflation can temporarily raise unemployment.

options.label: C
options.text: All six monetary policy goals are achieved simultaneously without any costs.
options.feedbackWrong: The lesson highlights short-run trade-offs. Simultaneous success is not what happens when the Bank raises rates to fight inflation.

options.label: D
options.text: The money supply automatically expands, so no further policy action is needed.
options.feedbackWrong: Raising the policy interest rate is a contractionary action; it does not automatically expand the money supply.

questions.ossdExpectation: Analyse various aspects of monetary policy in Canada and their impact on the economy.
questions.alignmentNote: Classifying money supply is part of monetary policy analysis in the Bank of Canada's operational toolkit.
questions.stemIntent: Assesses the hierarchy of monetary aggregates from narrowest (M0) to broadest (M2).
questions.commonMisconception: Students think M1 includes M2, or that M0/M1/M2 are unrelated categories.

options.label: A
options.text: M2 includes M1, which includes M0.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. M0 is physical cash, M1 adds demand deposits, and M2 adds money market shares and savings deposits.

options.label: B
options.text: M1 includes M2, which includes M0.
options.feedbackWrong: The order is wrong. M1 is narrower than M2; M2 contains M1, not the other way around.

options.label: C
options.text: M0 includes M1, which includes M2.
options.feedbackWrong: M0 is the narrowest measure, so it cannot include the broader M1 or M2 definitions.

options.label: D
options.text: M0, M1, and M2 are mutually exclusive categories.
options.feedbackWrong: Each broader definition builds on the previous one. M1 contains M0, and M2 contains M1.

questions.stem: A central bank decides to set a target for the interest rate while also trying to control the growth of a monetary aggregate. According to the lesson, this strategy is:
questions.successCriteria: Student knows that the Bank of Canada cannot precisely target both an interest rate and a monetary aggregate at the same time.
questions.ossdExpectation: Analyse various aspects of monetary policy in Canada and their impact on the economy.
questions.alignmentNote: Target selection criteria are part of the monetary policy operational framework.
questions.stemIntent: Verifies whether students know the incompatibility of simultaneous interest-rate and monetary-aggregate targeting.
questions.commonMisconception: Students believe a central bank can independently control both an interest rate and a monetary aggregate at the same time.

options.label: A
options.text: Impossible, because a central bank cannot precisely target both at the same time.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The lesson states a central bank can target either an interest rate or a monetary aggregate, but not both simultaneously.

options.label: B
options.text: Normal, because interest rates and monetary aggregates are independent tools.
options.feedbackWrong: They are not independent. Choosing one determines money-market conditions and makes the other endogenous.

options.label: C
options.text: Possible, if the aggregate target is set first and the interest rate target is then abandoned.
options.feedbackWrong: That would mean targeting only one of them. The strategy described in the stem tries to target both at once.

options.label: D
options.text: Required by the inflation-targeting framework since 1991.
options.feedbackWrong: Inflation targeting sets an inflation band, not a simultaneous interest-rate and monetary-aggregate target.

reteachModules.trigger: Student assumes all six monetary policy goals can be achieved simultaneously without short-run trade-offs.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes the Bank of Canada can simultaneously achieve high employment, steady growth, price stability, interest rate stability, financial market stability, and foreign exchange market stability with no costs. The student does not see that raising interest rates to curb inflation may temporarily increase unemployment.

miniLesson.explain: Canada’s monetary policy has six core objectives, but they can conflict in the short run. The lesson states that raising interest rates to curb inflation may temporarily increase unemployment. Price stability is the top priority because unanchored inflation disrupts long-term planning and creates social conflict. When the Bank of Canada raises rates by 300 basis points to cool demand and ease inflation, it accepts a possible short-term softening in employment as part of the trade-off.
miniLesson.example: Inflation is above the 1–3% target range. The Bank raises its policy interest rate. The higher rate cools demand and helps bring inflation back toward the 2% midpoint, but it also slows hiring, so unemployment may temporarily rise. This is a short-run trade-off between lower inflation and employment.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think: six goals, but not all at once — higher rates fight inflation but can temporarily cost jobs.

guidedPractice.prompt: How many core objectives does Canada’s monetary policy have, and can all of them be achieved simultaneously in the short run according to the lesson?
guidedPractice.answer: Canada’s monetary policy has six core objectives. The lesson says policy targets can conflict in the short run, so they cannot all be achieved at once.

guidedPractice.prompt: If the Bank of Canada raises the policy interest rate to lower inflation, what short-run effect on unemployment is the lesson most likely expecting, and why?
guidedPractice.answer: Unemployment may temporarily rise because raising interest rates to curb inflation can slow economic activity and hiring. This is a short-run trade-off between price stability and high employment.

guidedPractice.prompt: The Bank of Canada raised rates by 300 basis points to cool demand and ease inflation. Explain why this action helps achieve the inflation target but may also create a trade-off with employment.
guidedPractice.answer: The rate hikes cool domestic demand, which eases inflation toward the 1–3% target. But the same cooling can slow the labour market, so unemployment may temporarily increase. This illustrates the short-run conflict between price stability and high employment, making it impossible to achieve all six goals at once.

reteachModules.trigger: Student chooses an option that misplaces demand deposits, savings deposits, or money market shares among M0, M1, and M2, or forgets that M1 includes M0.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student treats M0, M1, and M2 as separate, unrelated categories instead of nested aggregates, so they may place demand deposits in M2 or omit cash from M1.

miniLesson.explain: Canada's money supply is classified into three nested definitions. M0 is physical cash only. M1 is M0 plus demand deposits. M2 is M1 plus money market shares and savings deposits. Therefore every component of M0 is also in M1, and every component of M1 is also in M2. When classifying, start with cash, then add demand deposits to get M1, then add money market shares and savings deposits to get M2.
miniLesson.example: Cash in circulation is M0. Once demand deposits are added to cash, that total becomes M1. Adding money market shares and savings deposits to M1 produces M2.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think nesting dolls: M0 is the smallest doll, M1 contains M0, and M2 contains M1.

guidedPractice.prompt: Cash is added to demand deposits to form which monetary aggregate?
guidedPractice.answer: M1, because M1 is M0 (physical cash) plus demand deposits.

guidedPractice.prompt: A classmate writes: 'M1 = M0 + money market shares + savings deposits.' Explain why this is incorrect using the M1 and M2 definitions.
guidedPractice.answer: It is wrong because M1 includes only M0 plus demand deposits. Money market shares and savings deposits are added at the M2 stage, so the correct relationships are M1 = M0 + demand deposits and M2 = M1 + money market shares + savings deposits.

reteachModules.trigger: A student incorrectly believes the Bank of Canada can simultaneously fix both the policy interest rate and the growth of a monetary aggregate like M1.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student thinks interest-rate targeting and monetary-aggregate targeting are independent tools that can be set at the same time, rather than mutually exclusive alternatives. This often comes from treating central bank actions as if they can directly control both the price and quantity of money without conflict.

miniLesson.explain: The central bank operates in the money market. When it sets a target for the interest rate, it must supply or absorb reserves to hold that rate; the quantity of money is then whatever the public and banks want at that rate. Conversely, if it commits to a specific growth rate for an aggregate like M1, it cannot also hold interest rates fixed—rates will rise or fall to keep money growth in line. Therefore, trying to target both would force contradictory actions. The Bank of Canada therefore chooses one operating target at a time, based on measurability, controllability, and predictable correlation with its final goals.
miniLesson.example: In the late 1970s and early 1980s (1975–1981), the Bank of Canada chose monetary aggregate targeting, gradually reducing M1 growth. It did not simultaneously fix a precise interest-rate target. Later, after 1991, it adopted explicit inflation targeting; within that framework, it uses the interest rate as its operating instrument. The shift between phases shows that the Bank could not pursue both at once.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: One lever, two dials: you can set the speed (money supply) or the wheel (interest rate), but not both at the same time. If you grab the wheel, the speed moves freely; if you hold the gas pedal fixed, the wheel turns.

guidedPractice.prompt: Fill in the blank: A central bank can target either an ______ or a ______, but not both at the same time.
Explain in your own words why the Bank of Canada cannot precisely target both the interest rate and a monetary aggregate at the same time.
guidedPractice.answer: If the Bank fixes the interest rate, it must adjust the money supply to meet demand at that rate, so the aggregate becomes whatever the market creates. If it fixed the aggregate, it would have to let the interest rate move to achieve that quantity. Trying to do both would require contradictory policies.

guidedPractice.prompt: During the 1975–1981 monetary aggregate targeting phase, the Bank of Canada gradually reduced M1 growth targets. Suppose someone argued the Bank should also keep the interest rate at a specific level. Using the lesson, explain why this would be impossible.
guidedPractice.answer: Targeting M1 growth means allowing interest rates to fluctuate to bring the money supply to the target level. If the Bank also tried to hold the interest rate fixed, it would have to buy or sell reserves to peg the rate, which would change the money supply and break the M1 target. Therefore it could not do both simultaneously.

reteachModules.trigger: The student believes inflation targeting works instantly and without output fluctuations, ignoring the long and variable lag inherent in monetary policy.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Inflation targeting is often misunderstood as an immediate, precise tool. In reality, monetary policy operates with long and variable lags, so a change in interest rates today affects output before it affects inflation, potentially creating short-run output fluctuations.

miniLesson.explain: The Bank of Canada's inflation-targeting framework—targeting 1–3% inflation with a 2% midpoint—has been in place since 1991. It is designed to keep long-run inflation expectations anchored near 2%, and it has generally succeeded over 30 years. However, monetary policy works with long and variable lags: when the Bank raises interest rates, it takes time for borrowing, spending, investment, and ultimately prices to respond. Because the lag is long and unpredictable, by the time the policy takes full effect, economic conditions may have changed, which can cause output to overshoot or undershoot. In the short run, this trade-off appears as fluctuations in output and employment.
miniLesson.example: The Bank of Canada raised rates by 300 basis points since March to cool domestic demand and ease inflation. These rate hikes did not instantly lower inflation; rather, they work gradually through the economy. The Bank also abandoned its 'transitory inflation' forecast after the Russia–Ukraine war pushed up commodity and supply chain costs, acknowledging that inflation would persist longer than initially expected. If inflation targeting worked instantly, there would be no need for a 300-basis-point campaign, and no risk of temporary output disruption.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of inflation targeting like steering a large ship: turning the wheel now only changes the ship's course much later. If you correct too late or too much, the ship may overshoot or wobble, even though you eventually reach the intended destination.

guidedPractice.prompt: Fill in the blanks: The Bank of Canada's inflation-targeting framework works with ________ and ________ lags, which can cause short-term output fluctuations.
Why can inflation targeting cause short-run output fluctuations even though long-run inflation expectations have stayed near 2% over 30 years?
guidedPractice.answer: Because monetary policy has long and variable lags—it affects output before it affects inflation, so by the time the policy takes effect, conditions may have changed, causing output to fluctuate temporarily.

guidedPractice.prompt: Explain how the Bank of Canada's 300-basis-point rate hikes since March illustrate the lag problem in inflation targeting. What specific warning did the Bank give to avoid a wage-price spiral?
guidedPractice.answer: The rate hikes were intended to cool domestic demand and ease inflation, but they take time to work. The Bank warned against a wage-price spiral and urged multi-year wage contracts aligned with inflation targets to avoid even sharper rate hikes, acknowledging that without coordinated expectations, inflation could remain higher for longer and require more painful adjustments.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects G7 members (including Canada and Italy) as participants in the 1985 Plaza Accord.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student confuses the G5 Plaza Accord with the later G7 Louvre Accord, incorrectly believing Canada and Italy were part of the 1985 agreement.

miniLesson.explain: The 1985 Plaza Accord was signed by the G5 countries: the United States, United Kingdom, France, West Germany, and Japan. Canada and Italy were NOT part of this agreement. They later joined the 1987 Louvre Accord, which expanded the group to the G7. The Plaza Accord aimed to depreciate the US dollar after it had appreciated 50% from 1980 to 1985.
miniLesson.example: Imagine a five-member club (G5) meets in 1985 to fix a currency problem: the US dollar is too strong and hurting exports. They agree to coordinate intervention. Canada and Italy are not club members yet, so they do not attend. That club later expands to seven members (G7) in 1987 for the Louvre Accord.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Plaza = 5 (no Canada, no Italy). Louvre = 7 (adds Canada and Italy). Think: 'Plaza has five towers, Louvre has seven art wings.'

guidedPractice.prompt: Which five countries signed the 1985 Plaza Accord?
guidedPractice.answer: The United States, United Kingdom, France, West Germany, and Japan.

guidedPractice.prompt: Why is it incorrect to list Canada and Italy as Plaza Accord members?
guidedPractice.answer: Because the Plaza Accord was a G5 agreement. Canada and Italy were not part of it; they only joined at the 1987 Louvre Accord as part of the G7.

guidedPractice.prompt: How does the membership difference between the Plaza Accord and the Louvre Accord help explain their different outcomes?
guidedPractice.answer: The Plaza Accord (G5, 1985) succeeded because unified signals from five major economies deterred speculators, leading to a roughly 35% depreciation of the US dollar by 1987. The Louvre Accord (G7, 1987) included Canada and Italy but failed to stabilise exchange rates, and the global stock market crashed later that year. The membership difference reflects the historical phase: Plaza was the successful G5 intervention, while the expanded G7 Louvre could not repeat that success.

reteachModules.trigger: Student answers a diagnostic question about the 1987 Louvre Accord by claiming it successfully stabilised exchange rates and prevented the 1987 stock market crash.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student confuses the Louvre Accord with the Plaza Accord's success. The Louvre Accord was a G7 attempt to halt the dollar's unplanned depreciation, but it failed to stabilise exchange rates and was followed by the 1987 global stock market crash.

miniLesson.explain: The 1985 Plaza Accord succeeded because the G5 countries coordinated a depreciation of the US dollar, which fell roughly 35% by 1987. By 1987, the dollar's continued decline was unplanned, so the G7 (G5 plus Canada and Italy) signed the Louvre Accord to try to halt it. Unlike the Plaza Accord, the Louvre Accord failed to stabilise exchange rates, and the 1987 global stock market crash followed. Therefore, the Louvre Accord is an example of coordinated intervention that did not achieve its goal.
miniLesson.example: After the dollar appreciated 50% from 1980 to 1985, the Plaza Accord produced a coordinated depreciation of about 35% by 1987. The 1987 Louvre Accord tried to stop further dollar declines but did not stabilise exchange rates; it preceded the 1987 global stock market crash.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Plaza pushed the dollar down and succeeded; Louvre tried to hold the line, but lost it—and the crash followed.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which countries met at the 1987 Louvre Accord, and what was their goal?
guidedPractice.answer: The G7 (G5 plus Canada and Italy) met. Their goal was to halt the dollar's unplanned depreciation.

guidedPractice.prompt: Compare the outcomes of the 1985 Plaza Accord and the 1987 Louvre Accord.
guidedPractice.answer: The Plaza Accord succeeded: the US dollar depreciated roughly 35% by 1987. The Louvre Accord failed to stabilise exchange rates and was followed by the 1987 global stock market crash.

guidedPractice.prompt: Why does the failure of the Louvre Accord matter for understanding international monetary coordination?
guidedPractice.answer: It shows that even coordinated G7 intervention can fail. The Plaza Accord worked partly because unified G5 signals deterred speculators, but the Louvre Accord's failure just before the 1987 crash demonstrates that coordination alone does not guarantee stable exchange rates.

options: All six monetary policy objectives will be achieved at the same time without any costs.
Inflation will fall immediately, and employment will remain completely unaffected.
The higher interest rate will cool demand and ease inflation, but unemployment may temporarily rise.
The higher interest rate will only affect the foreign exchange market and not domestic inflation or employment.

questions.stem: Explain why the Bank of Canada’s pursuit of price stability may conflict with the goal of high employment in the short run. Use the example of a 300-basis-point rate hike in your explanation.
questions.rubric: Responses should state that price stability is prioritized and that raising interest rates to reduce inflation can slow economic activity and hiring, temporarily increasing unemployment. Strong answers may note that the Bank cannot achieve all six objectives simultaneously and that rate hikes are accepted despite this short-run trade-off.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly. For the open-ended question, the response must clearly identify the short-run conflict between price stability and employment and explain how rate hikes can lower inflation but temporarily raise unemployment.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the Bank of Canada’s classification of the money supply?
options: M1 = M0 + demand deposits; M2 = M1 + savings deposits + money market shares
M1 = M0 + savings deposits; M2 = M1 + demand deposits + money market shares
M1 = cash + savings deposits; M2 = M1 + demand deposits
M0 = cash + demand deposits; M1 = M0 + savings deposits

questions.stem: Suppose an economy has physical cash of $60 billion, demand deposits of $140 billion, savings deposits of $200 billion, and money market shares of $100 billion. Calculate M0, M1, and M2, and explain which items are added at each stage.
questions.rubric: States M0 = $60B (cash only); M1 = M0 + demand deposits = $200B; M2 = M1 + savings deposits + money market shares = $500B. Explanation must show M1 contains M0 plus demand deposits, and M2 contains M1 plus savings deposits and money market shares, demonstrating the nested structure.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly. Q1 must select option 0. Q2 must compute M0 = $60B, M1 = $200B, M2 = $500B, and explain that M1 = M0 + demand deposits, M2 = M1 + savings deposits + money market shares, with M0 nested in M1 and M1 nested in M2.

questions.stem: Which situation best illustrates why the Bank of Canada must choose between an interest rate target and a monetary aggregate target?
options: Trying to keep the interest rate at 2% while also limiting M1 growth to 3% would require buying and selling reserves in opposite directions at the same time.
The Bank of Canada has only one physical tool, such as a printing press, so it can only ever control one variable.
Interest rates and monetary aggregates are too volatile to be measured accurately in real time, so the Bank cannot track both.
Both targets are necessary for controlling inflation, so the Bank must somehow use both simultaneously.

questions.stem: Suppose the Bank of Canada announced that it would keep the policy interest rate at 2.5% for the next year and also ensure that M2 grows at exactly 4% during the same period. Using your knowledge from this lesson, explain why this policy package is impossible and what the Bank would have to do if it tried to enforce both targets.
questions.rubric: The student should explain that the interest rate and money supply are jointly determined in the money market. If the Bank pegs the interest rate, it must adjust the money supply through open market operations to offset changes in money demand, so M2 growth cannot be independently fixed. If it locks in M2 growth at 4%, the interest rate must be left free to move to equilibrate the market. Trying to do both would require contradictory open market operations (e.g., buying securities to keep the rate low while selling securities to slow money growth). The answer should clearly indicate the mutual exclusivity of the two targets and mention the need to choose one operating target.

retestCards.passRule: To pass, the student must select the correct answer for Q1 (index 0) and for Q2 provide a response that demonstrates understanding that the central bank cannot simultaneously enforce both a fixed interest rate and a fixed monetary aggregate, ideally explaining the contradictory open-market operations that would be required. The response should be at least two sentences and explicitly reference the trade-off or the need to choose one target.

questions.stem: The Bank of Canada raises its policy interest rate today to bring inflation from 4% back to the 2% midpoint. Based on the inflation-targeting framework, which short-run effect is most likely?
options: Inflation falls immediately because markets adjust their expectations right away.
Output and employment rise immediately because the rate hike stimulates investment.
The full effect on inflation is delayed; output may slow or fluctuate before prices respond.
There is no effect on the economy until the next rate announcement.

questions.stem: Explain in two or three sentences why the Bank of Canada's 300-basis-point rate hikes do not instantly lower inflation. In your answer, name the type of lag involved and describe one possible short-run consequence.
questions.rubric: Student must state that monetary policy has a 'long and variable lag' (or equivalent phrasing such as 'long/variable delay') before affecting inflation. They must also mention that output or employment may fluctuate or slow in the short run. Acceptable: rate hikes affect borrowing/spending gradually, and by the time inflation responds, economic conditions may have changed, causing temporary output fluctuations.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly. For the open-ended question, the response must include references to monetary policy lags (long and variable) and a short-run output fluctuation or slowdown.

questions.stem: Which two countries were added to the group when the 1987 Louvre Accord expanded the Plaza Accord's membership from G5 to G7?
options: Canada and Italy
Canada and Australia
Mexico and Italy
Japan and West Germany

questions.stem: Briefly explain the difference in membership between the 1985 Plaza Accord and the 1987 Louvre Accord, and state one reason why the Plaza Accord was more successful than the Louvre Accord in stabilizing the US dollar.
questions.rubric: Answer must correctly state that the Plaza Accord was G5 (US, UK, France, West Germany, Japan) while the Louvre Accord was G7 (adding Canada and Italy). A valid reason for Plaza's success: unified G5 signals deterred speculators from betting against sovereign intervention, leading to a roughly 35% depreciation of the dollar by 1987; the Louvre Accord failed to stabilise exchange rates, preceding the 1987 crash. Accept any reason that shows understanding of the coordinated intervention signal.

retestCards.passRule: Student must answer the single-choice question correctly and provide a response to the open-ended question that correctly identifies the G5 vs G7 membership and explains the Plaza Accord's success. Partial credit may be given, but the student must demonstrate understanding of the membership difference.

questions.stem: What was the actual outcome of the 1987 Louvre Accord?
options: It successfully stabilised exchange rates and prevented the 1987 global stock market crash.
It failed to stabilise exchange rates and was followed by the 1987 global stock market crash.
It coordinated a 35% depreciation of the US dollar by 1987.
It was a G5 agreement to appreciate the US dollar.

questions.stem: Compare the 1985 Plaza Accord and the 1987 Louvre Accord. Why did the Plaza Accord succeed while the Louvre Accord failed? Refer to the membership and the economic context of each accord.
questions.rubric: The response must correctly state that the Plaza Accord (G5: US, UK, France, West Germany, Japan) succeeded in coordinating a depreciation of the US dollar, which fell roughly 35% by 1987. The Louvre Accord (G7: G5 plus Canada and Italy) aimed to halt the dollar's unplanned depreciation but failed to stabilise exchange rates and immediately preceded the 1987 global stock market crash. The answer should clearly distinguish the outcomes and show understanding that the Louvre Accord was a failed attempt, not a success.

retestCards.passRule: Answer Q1 correctly (option B) and provide a Q2 response that explicitly states the Louvre Accord failed to stabilise exchange rates and was followed by the 1987 crash, while correctly describing the Plaza Accord's success.

dashboardFormat.objective: Canada’s monetary policy has six core objectives: high employment, steady economic growth, price stability, interest rate stability, financial market stability, and foreign exchange market stability.；Policy targets can conflict in the short run; for example, raising interest rates to curb inflation may temporarily increase unemployment.；High employment targets the natural unemployment rate to avoid lost output and human distress.

learningGoals.statement: Analyze the Bank of Canada's monetary policy objectives and explain short-run trade-offs among them.
Classify monetary aggregates (M0, M1, M2) and explain why a central bank cannot simultaneously target an interest rate and a monetary aggregate.
Evaluate Canada's inflation-targeting framework, including its lags, and apply the Plaza and Louvre Accords to coordinated exchange-rate intervention.

cards.question: The Bank of Canada raises its policy interest rate to reduce inflation. According to the lesson, which short-run consequence is most likely?
options: Unemployment immediately falls because lower inflation boosts consumer spending.
Unemployment may temporarily rise, reflecting a trade-off between lower inflation and employment.
All six monetary policy goals are achieved simultaneously without any costs.
The money supply automatically expands, so no further policy action is needed.
cards.diagnosis: Checks whether students understand that monetary policy goals conflict in the short run, specifically the unemployment cost of disinflation.
misconceptions: Disinflation usually does not immediately boost employment; the lesson explicitly notes that raising rates to curb inflation may temporarily increase unemployment.
✓ Correct. The lesson states that policy targets can conflict in the short run; disinflation can temporarily raise unemployment.
The lesson highlights short-run trade-offs. Simultaneous success is not what happens when the Bank raises rates to fight inflation.
Raising the policy interest rate is a contractionary action; it does not automatically expand the money supply.
cards.successCriteria: Student recognizes that lowering inflation through higher interest rates can temporarily raise unemployment.
cards.ossdExpectation: Analyse various aspects of monetary policy in Canada and their impact on the economy.
cards.alignmentNote: Monetary policy goals and their trade-offs are central to analysing the Bank of Canada's monetary policy.
cards.commonMisconception: All six monetary policy goals can be achieved simultaneously without any trade-offs, or inflation control has no employment cost.

cards.question: Based on the diagram, which statement correctly describes the relationship among Canada's money supply definitions?
options: M2 includes M1, which includes M0.
M1 includes M2, which includes M0.
M0 includes M1, which includes M2.
M0, M1, and M2 are mutually exclusive categories.
cards.diagnosis: Assesses the hierarchy of monetary aggregates from narrowest (M0) to broadest (M2).
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. M0 is physical cash, M1 adds demand deposits, and M2 adds money market shares and savings deposits.
The order is wrong. M1 is narrower than M2; M2 contains M1, not the other way around.
M0 is the narrowest measure, so it cannot include the broader M1 or M2 definitions.
Each broader definition builds on the previous one. M1 contains M0, and M2 contains M1.
cards.successCriteria: Student understands that M0 is the narrowest measure, M1 includes M0, and M2 includes M1.
cards.ossdExpectation: Analyse various aspects of monetary policy in Canada and their impact on the economy.
cards.alignmentNote: Classifying money supply is part of monetary policy analysis in the Bank of Canada's operational toolkit.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think M1 includes M2, or that M0/M1/M2 are unrelated categories.

cards.question: A central bank decides to set a target for the interest rate while also trying to control the growth of a monetary aggregate. According to the lesson, this strategy is:
options: Impossible, because a central bank cannot precisely target both at the same time.
Normal, because interest rates and monetary aggregates are independent tools.
Possible, if the aggregate target is set first and the interest rate target is then abandoned.
Required by the inflation-targeting framework since 1991.
cards.diagnosis: Verifies whether students know the incompatibility of simultaneous interest-rate and monetary-aggregate targeting.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. The lesson states a central bank can target either an interest rate or a monetary aggregate, but not both simultaneously.
They are not independent. Choosing one determines money-market conditions and makes the other endogenous.
That would mean targeting only one of them. The strategy described in the stem tries to target both at once.
Inflation targeting sets an inflation band, not a simultaneous interest-rate and monetary-aggregate target.
cards.successCriteria: Student knows that the Bank of Canada cannot precisely target both an interest rate and a monetary aggregate at the same time.
cards.ossdExpectation: Analyse various aspects of monetary policy in Canada and their impact on the economy.
cards.alignmentNote: Target selection criteria are part of the monetary policy operational framework.
cards.commonMisconception: Students believe a central bank can independently control both an interest rate and a monetary aggregate at the same time.

cards.question: In one or two sentences, explain why Canada's inflation-targeting framework can cause short-run output fluctuations even though it has kept long-run inflation expectations near 2%.
cards.diagnosis: Checks understanding of the lag disadvantage of inflation targeting, especially the risk of output fluctuations.
cards.successCriteria: Student mentions the long and variable lags of monetary policy and that policy hits output before inflation, potentially causing fluctuations.
cards.ossdExpectation: Analyse various aspects of monetary policy in Canada and their impact on the economy.
cards.alignmentNote: Evaluating the inflation-targeting framework's disadvantages is part of monetary policy analysis.
cards.commonMisconception: Students believe inflation targeting works instantly and without any cost to output.

cards.question: Which countries participated in the 1985 Plaza Accord?
options: The G5: US, UK, France, West Germany, and Japan.
The G7: US, UK, France, West Germany, Japan, Canada, and Italy.
Only Canada and Italy.
Only the US and Japan.
cards.diagnosis: Confirms that the Plaza Accord was a G5 agreement, not a G7 agreement.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct. The Plaza Accord was a G5 agreement. Canada and Italy joined only in the later 1987 Louvre Accord.
That is the G7, which met at the 1987 Louvre Accord, not the 1985 Plaza Accord.
Canada and Italy were not original Plaza Accord members; they were part of the later Louvre Accord.
The Plaza Accord involved the G5 countries, not just the US and Japan.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies the G5 members: US, UK, France, West Germany, and Japan.
cards.ossdExpectation: Analyse the impact of some key international economic events and developments as well as various responses to them.
cards.alignmentNote: The Plaza Accord is a key international economic event directly impacting exchange-rate policy and Canadian economic context.
cards.commonMisconception: Students include Canada and Italy because they later joined the G7 Louvre Accord.
